meta.blurb: Follow Mina and her grandfather Tomas through one year in one old forest, from a falling acorn to a new one planted. Along the way you will meet roots, fungi, giant trees and the quiet signals that may pass between them.
meta.bible: Mina: a curious girl of about ten who asks why about everything. Tomas: her grandfather, a retired forester, patient and kind. They walk through one old forest in every season of one year, from Autumn to Autumn. The forest has Oak, Beech and Pine trees and a Stream. Suzanne Simard: a real forest scientist whose research on Mycorrhizal networks and Mother trees is real, though how much it matters for a whole forest is still Debated. Bristlecone pine: lives more than four thousand years, the oldest nearly five thousand. Redwood: Coast redwood of California by the Pacific, the tallest over one hundred Metres. Key terms: Acorn, Seedling, Jay, Chlorophyll, Photosynthesis, Stomata, Xylem, Phloem, Sap, Bark, Rings, Canopy, Understorey, Evergreen, Catkins, Fungi, Fungus, Mycorrhizal, Phosphorus, Deadwood, Carbon, Oxygen, Springtails, Hub trees, Nurse log. Voice: wondering, clear and kind. The science is real and hedged where scientists disagree: no invented numbers, studies or quotes.

beats.scene: Mina and her grandfather Tomas walk into a golden autumn forest at dawn
beats.summary: On an autumn morning, Mina and her grandfather Tomas begin a year of walking through the forest.

beats.scene: A huge old oak drops acorns onto leaves while Mina watches
beats.summary: The oak lets its acorns fall, and Tomas explains that each acorn is a seed.

beats.scene: A jay carries an acorn in its beak between tree trunks
beats.summary: A jay buries acorns, and the ones it forgets may grow into new oaks.

beats.scene: Mina kneels by an acorn in damp soil and marks it with a stick
beats.summary: Mina finds one acorn in the soil and marks the spot to watch it through the year.

beats.scene: Mina holds a yellow leaf up against red and orange trees
beats.summary: Leaves change colour in autumn as the green chlorophyll breaks down.

beats.scene: Yellow leaves drift down around Tomas as he holds out a hand
beats.summary: A tree seals the base of each leaf and lets it fall to survive the winter.

beats.scene: Mina lifts damp leaves and finds worms and tiny beetles beneath
beats.summary: Worms, beetles and fungi break down fallen leaves and turn them into soil.

beats.scene: Tomas points up through treetops, small trees and ferns below
beats.summary: Tomas describes the layers of a forest: canopy, understorey and floor.

beats.scene: Mina rests her palm on the deep ridges of oak bark
beats.summary: Bark works like skin, protecting the living wood from cold, insects and sometimes fire.

beats.scene: Mina counts the rings on a fresh stump with her fingertip
beats.summary: A tree adds one ring of wood each year, so the rings tell its age.

beats.scene: Tomas points to wide and narrow rings as Mina leans close
beats.summary: Wide rings usually mean good years and narrow rings hard years, so rings record the weather.

beats.scene: Mina and Tomas in wool hats walk through snow between bare trunks
beats.summary: Snow falls, and the forest rests through winter.

beats.scene: Snow lies on dark green pine branches as Mina looks up
beats.summary: Evergreens keep narrow, waxy needles through winter.

beats.scene: Mina brushes snow from her marker stick above the buried acorn
beats.summary: Many seeds need a spell of cold before they sprout, so the acorn waits.

beats.scene: A squirrel digs in deep snow while a deer watches nearby
beats.summary: Animals live through winter, and squirrels forget nuts that may sprout.

beats.scene: Tomas bends a snowy twig to show Mina its tight brown buds
beats.summary: Buds already hold the folded leaves of next spring.

beats.scene: A woodpecker clings to a tall grey dead trunk full of holes
beats.summary: A standing dead tree gives homes and food to many creatures.

beats.scene: Tomas kneels in snow and shows Mina a root wrapped in pale threads
beats.summary: Tomas shows Mina the fungal threads around roots, called mycorrhizal.

beats.scene: White fungal threads wrap an oak root in dark soil
beats.summary: Trees and fungi trade sugar for water and minerals.

beats.scene: Pale threads link the roots of several trees underground
beats.summary: Fungal threads can join trees, and scientists have measured substances moving between them.

beats.scene: Mina looks up at the oldest oak with small seedlings at its base
beats.summary: Suzanne Simard and others studied old hub trees, and some scientists think these may help seedlings.

beats.scene: Mina writes in a notebook while sitting on a snowy log with Tomas
beats.summary: Scientists still disagree about how much the networks matter in a whole forest.

beats.scene: Soft rain falls on green buds as Mina and Tomas walk
beats.summary: Spring arrives, sap rises and the buds swell.

beats.scene: Mina crouches by the stick where a pale root leaves the acorn
beats.summary: Mina's acorn splits open and a root pushes out first.

beats.scene: A pale root grows down through dark soil, covered in fine hairs
beats.summary: Root hairs take in water and minerals.

beats.scene: Tomas draws wide spreading roots in the dust with a stick
beats.summary: Roots sense wetter soil and spread wide and shallow.

beats.scene: A small oak seedling with two leaves stands in the old oak's shade
beats.summary: A shoot rises into the deep shade, and seedlings may wait there for light.

beats.scene: Fresh bright green leaves unfold on the oak as Mina looks up
beats.summary: The big oak opens its new leaves.

beats.scene: Sunlight shines through green oak leaves onto Mina's upturned face
beats.summary: Photosynthesis turns light, water and carbon dioxide into sugar and releases oxygen.

beats.scene: Mina studies the underside of a leaf with a magnifying glass
beats.summary: Tiny pores called stomata let gases in and out and let water vapour escape.

beats.scene: Tomas points up a tall trunk while Mina follows with her eyes
beats.summary: Water climbs through the xylem, pulled by evaporation from the leaves.

beats.scene: Mina touches the bark of the oak while Tomas watches
beats.summary: Sugar travels down through the phloem, just under the bark.

beats.scene: A blue tit carries moss to a nest hole while bees visit blossom
beats.summary: Spring fills the branches with nesting birds, bees and wind-blown oak pollen.

beats.scene: A green caterpillar chews a lacy hole in a young oak leaf
beats.summary: Caterpillars eat young leaves, and trees defend themselves with chemicals.

beats.scene: Mina sniffs a torn leaf beside a neighbouring tree with green leaves
beats.summary: Some trees release chemicals when chewed, and neighbours may respond, though scientists debate what it means.

beats.scene: A tiny wasp lands on a chewed leaf beside a caterpillar
beats.summary: The same chemicals may attract wasps and birds that attack the caterpillars.

beats.scene: Mina and Tomas rest in deep green shade beside a sparkling stream
beats.summary: In midsummer, the forest is cooler than the fields outside.

beats.scene: Mina and Tomas shelter under rock as wind bends the treetops
beats.summary: A summer storm shows that wind makes trees thicker and stronger.

beats.scene: Tomas touches a blackened pine trunk with green shoots at its base
beats.summary: An old fire scar shows how some trees and plants survive and recover.

beats.scene: A huge beech lies on the ground, its roots lifted like a wall
beats.summary: The storm has felled a giant beech and opened a gap of light.

beats.scene: A mossy fallen log with ferns, mushrooms and small seedlings on top
beats.summary: The fallen tree decays slowly and feeds new life.

beats.scene: Tomas opens a book showing a twisted ancient pine on a dry mountain
beats.summary: Tomas tells Mina about the bristlecone pines, the oldest known trees.

beats.scene: Giant redwoods in morning fog tower over tiny walkers below
beats.summary: Tomas tells Mina about the coast redwoods, the tallest trees.

beats.scene: Mina and Tomas walk through falling gold leaves toward the oak
beats.summary: Autumn returns, and Mina sees the forest as a connected community.

beats.scene: Mina kneels beside a small oak seedling and the old grey stick
beats.summary: Mina's seedling has survived the year but is still very small.

beats.scene: Mina presses her hands to a trunk while sunlight warms the leaves
beats.summary: Trees store carbon, and forests matter for the climate.

beats.scene: Mina and Tomas watch a deer drink at a clear forest stream
beats.summary: Forests also shelter animals, hold soil and keep water clean.

beats.scene: Mina and neighbours plant a young tree in a sunny field
beats.summary: People can plant the right trees in the right places and protect old forests.

beats.scene: Mina steps carefully along a narrow path past a fallen branch
beats.summary: Tomas gives two rules: leave deadwood, and walk lightly.

beats.scene: Mina presses an acorn into the earth while Tomas smiles beside her
beats.summary: Mina plants her own acorn, joining the long work of the forest.

B1B2: Mina has come to the old forest with her grandfather Tomas, who used to be a forester. He has promised to walk with her through every season of one whole year.
The oak above them is very old, and in autumn it lets go of its acorns. Each acorn is a seed, and inside it a tiny tree is waiting.
A jay lands beside them and fills its throat with acorns before flying off. It will bury them in different places, and the ones it forgets may grow into new oaks.
Mina finds one acorn lying half hidden in the soft soil. She pushes a stick in beside it, because she wants to see what happens to it this year.
Leaves are green because they hold chlorophyll, a substance that catches sunlight. In autumn the chlorophyll breaks down, and the yellow and orange colours that were hiding underneath begin to show.
Before winter, the tree grows a thin layer of cells across the base of each leaf stalk. The leaf is sealed off, and it drifts down to the ground.
Under the fallen leaves, worms, beetles and fungi are already at work. They break the leaves into small pieces and turn them into dark, rich soil that feeds the trees.
Tomas explains that a forest has layers, like a house with floors. The canopy is the high roof of leaves, the understorey holds smaller trees and shrubs, and the forest floor is below.
Mina puts her hand on the rough bark of the oak. Like skin, it protects the living wood inside from cold, insects, fungi and sometimes even fire.
They find a stump where a tree was cut down, and Mina counts its rings. Each year the tree adds one new ring of wood, so the number of rings is the tree's age.
Mina notices that the rings are not all the same width. In a wet, warm year a tree usually grows a wide ring, but in a dry year the ring is thin.
Winter has arrived, and thick snow settles softly on all the branches. The forest is very still, as if it were asleep, although Tomas says that it is only resting.
Some trees, like pines and spruces, do not lose all their leaves. Their needles are narrow and have a waxy coat, which helps them keep water and shake off snow.
Deep under the snow, Mina's acorn lies in the dark and waits. Many tree seeds need a spell of cold before they will sprout, which stops them from waking up too early.
Many animals stay in the forest all through the long winter. A squirrel digs through the snow for the nuts it buried in autumn, and some of the nuts it never finds will sprout.
Tomas bends a branch toward Mina to show her the small buds on it. The leaves for next spring are already folded inside, packed tightly and protected by tough scales.
Not every tree standing in the forest is alive. A dead trunk full of holes gives woodpeckers, owls and many insects a place to make a home.
Tomas kneels and gently lifts a little soil beside a root. It is wrapped in fine white threads, which belong to fungi that live in the soil.
Mycorrhizal fungi and the trees they live with trade with each other. The tree gives the fungus sugar from its leaves, and the fungus brings water and minerals from the soil.
Fungal threads can also link the roots of different trees. In experiments, scientists have measured sugars and other chemicals moving from one tree to another.

A scientist named Suzanne Simard, and others, have studied old trees that are strongly linked to many neighbours. Some scientists think these hub trees, sometimes called mother trees, may help young seedlings that grow in their shade.
Tomas is careful to add that this is an exciting but debated area. Scientists agree that fungal networks exist, yet they still disagree about how much they matter for a whole forest.
As the days grow longer and warmer, the trees wake up. Sap begins to rise, the buds swell, and the forest slowly turns from brown to green.
Mina kneels by her stick and finds her acorn split open. A small white root has pushed out of it and is already heading down into the soil.
Behind its tip, the young root is covered with fine hairs. They take in water and minerals from the soil, and the root grows longer every day.
Roots can sense where the soil is wetter, and they tend to grow in that direction. A tree's roots often spread out wider than its branches, and most of them lie in the top layer of soil.
A small green shoot rises from the acorn and opens its first leaves. It stands in the shade of the big oak, where very little light reaches it.
High in the canopy, the big oak opens its new leaves. They are bright, soft and small at first, but they will soon be the tree's factory for making food.
Leaves make their food by a very clever process called photosynthesis. Using the energy of sunlight, they turn water and carbon dioxide from the air into sugar, and they release oxygen.
Under each leaf there are tiny pores called stomata. They open to let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out, but water vapour escapes through them as well.
Water travels from the roots to the leaves through very thin tubes in the wood, called xylem. As water evaporates from the leaves, it pulls more water up behind it, like a drink through a straw.
The sugar made in the leaves must reach the rest of the tree. It flows down through another set of tubes, called phloem, just under the bark.
Spring is a busy time up in the branches. Birds build nests, bees visit the blossom of other trees, and the oak hangs out long yellow catkins that let the wind carry its pollen.
Soft young leaves are tasty, and caterpillars arrive to eat them. Mina finds a leaf full of holes, and Tomas explains that trees cannot run away from hungry insects.

When insects chew their leaves, some trees release chemicals into the air. In some experiments, neighbouring trees that detected these chemicals made more defences in their own leaves, as if they had been warned.
The same chemicals can also work like a call for help. Some tiny wasps and some birds are drawn to the smell of a chewed leaf, and they attack the caterpillars.
By midsummer, the fields outside the forest are hot and dry. Under the trees it is cooler, because the leaves block the sun and the water they release cools the air.
A summer storm sweeps through the forest, and the tall trunks sway in the wind. Trees that are pushed by wind often grow thicker trunks and roots, so every storm is also a kind of training.
On the far side of the hill, they come to a place where a fire burned many years ago. The thick bark of some trees protected them, and young trees now grow between the blackened trunks.
The storm has brought down a huge old beech, and its roots stand up like a wall of earth. Where it fell, there is a gap in the canopy, and sunlight reaches the floor for the first time in decades.
Months later, the fallen beech is covered in moss, mushrooms and beetles. As it slowly rots, it feeds the soil, and tiny new trees sprout along its back.

One evening, Tomas shows Mina a book about bristlecone pines, which grow on dry, windy mountains in the western United States. Some of them have lived for more than four thousand years, and the oldest known are nearly five thousand years old.

Turning the page, Tomas shows Mina the coast redwoods of California, where the tallest known trees are over one hundred metres high. They live where ocean fog drifts in, and their leaves can take in some of that fog as water.
Autumn has come around again, and the oak is dropping its leaves once more. Mina now sees a forest where she once saw only trees, and she knows how much goes on beneath the colours.

Mina finds her seedling beside the old stick, a year older and a little taller than her hand. Oaks grow slowly at first, and Tomas says it may take many years before it reaches the light of the canopy.
Forests also play an important part in the world's climate. As trees grow, they take carbon dioxide out of the air and store the carbon in their wood, their roots and the soil.
Mina learns that forests do much more than store carbon in their wood. They shelter animals, hold the soil in place with their roots, and help keep streams clean.

Tomas says that planting trees helps, especially the right kinds in the right places. Protecting the old forests is just as important, because their soil, fungi and ancient trees cannot easily be replaced.
On their last walk, Tomas gives Mina two simple rules. Leave deadwood where it lies, because many creatures live in it, and walk lightly, because crushed soil is hard on roots.
Mina picks up a good acorn from the path and plants it in a sunny gap at the edge of the forest. She may never see it grow old, but Tomas says that a forest is made by people who plant for others.
C1C2: On a bright autumn morning, Mina followed her grandfather Tomas, a retired forester, along a path that led from the last field into the first shade of the trees. He had promised to walk with her through every season of one year, so that she might see how a forest truly lives and changes. Everything he was about to tell her, he said, had been found out by patient scientists with notebooks, and she was welcome to ask about any of it.

Above them stood an oak so old that Mina could not reach around its trunk, and in autumn it let its acorns drop like small brown raindrops. Every acorn is a seed, Tomas explained, a sleeping baby tree packed together with a little food to live on until it can find light. Most of them, he added, would never grow into trees at all, for there are far more acorns than there is room in the forest.

A jay swept down from the branches, gathered several acorns in its throat and beak, and flew off between the trunks to hide them in the ground for winter. Birds like this usually forget some of the seeds they bury, Tomas said, and so a forest is partly planted by creatures that simply lose track of their own supplies. Mina watched it go and wondered how many of the great oaks around her had begun life in exactly that way.

Mina knelt beside the trunk and found a single acorn already half sunk into the damp soil, its shell still shining. She pushed a stick in beside it so that she could find it again, and made a quiet promise to visit it in every season of the year. It was a small beginning, but she felt as though she were holding a very large secret.

The green of a leaf comes from chlorophyll, the pigment that catches sunlight, and as the days shorten the tree stops making it and takes back what it can. Yellow and orange pigments, which were there all summer behind the green, are suddenly revealed. In some trees a red pigment is made afresh in autumn, and scientists are still working out exactly why.

Late in autumn, a tree builds a thin layer of cells where each leaf stalk meets the twig, and it seals the wound as the leaf lets go. Broad leaves would catch snow and lose precious water in the cold, dry air, Tomas said, so dropping them is a way of surviving the winter. Soon the whole floor of the wood was a thick, rustling carpet, and every step Mina took sent up a smell of earth.

When Mina lifted a handful of leaves, she found a busy, hidden crowd of worms, beetles, springtails and threads of fungus slowly taking the leaf apart. Nothing in a forest is wasted, Tomas said, because what one year drops, the soil returns to the roots as food for the next. She laid the leaves back as carefully as a blanket over a sleeping child, so that the small workers beneath could go on.

Standing in a clearing, Tomas drew the forest in the air with his hands, starting with the canopy, the sunlit roof of leaves where the tallest trees meet the sky. Beneath it, he said, lies the understorey of young trees and shrubs, and below that the dim floor of moss, ferns and fallen leaves, and each layer has its own light and its own animals. A seedling on the floor must live for years on scraps of light, waiting for its chance.

The bark felt like cracked leather under Mina's palm, a rugged coat made of dead cells that shields the living layers beneath from frost, hungry insects, rot and sometimes even fire. Just under it, Tomas said, runs a thin layer where the tree really grows, adding a little new wood and a little new bark every year. A tree, he told her, is a living thing wearing the history of its own protection.

Beside the path lay a freshly cut stump, and Mina bent over it, counting the dark and pale circles with her fingertip. A tree adds a new layer of wood around its trunk every growing season, Tomas explained, so the rings, counted from the centre outwards, tell you how many years it lived. She counted sixty-one rings, and then she stood very still for a moment, thinking of everything that had happened in those years.

Some of the rings were wide and pale and others were narrow and tight, and Tomas said that they were a diary the tree had written without meaning to. A wide ring usually means a good year of water and warmth, a thin one a hard year, and scientists compare the patterns from many old trees to learn what the weather was like long before anyone measured it. Mina touched the narrowest ring with one finger and wondered what that long-ago year had been like for the tree.

When the first snow came, Mina and Tomas walked in wool hats and thick boots through a forest that had gone almost silent. The broad-leaved trees stood bare, their growth slowed to a crawl, and Tomas called it a rest rather than a sleep, because deep inside the wood a great deal was quietly going on. Mina's breath rose in small white clouds between the trunks, and the only sound was the creak of her boots on the snow.

Among the bare oaks stood a group of pines, still dark green, because evergreen trees keep their needles for several years rather than dropping them all each autumn. The needles are narrow, with a waxy coat that limits water loss, and the sloping branches let the snow slide away before its weight can do any harm. Even so, Tomas noted, an evergreen sheds some of its oldest needles every year.

Mina brushed the snow from the top of her marker stick and pictured the acorn lying in the cold dark below it. Many kinds of tree seed need a long spell of cold before they are able to sprout, Tomas said, a built-in safeguard that keeps them from waking during a mild week in the middle of winter. The seed, in its own way, was counting the days until spring, though it had no eyes to see the snow.

Tracks crossed the snow in every direction, and Mina followed those of a squirrel to a spot where it had dug down to a nut buried weeks before. Squirrels hide a great many nuts, Tomas said, and the ones that are forgotten may be left to sprout when the weather warms. Deer, foxes and owls were out there too, he added, and the winter forest was never as empty as it looked.

Tomas bent a bare twig down so that Mina could see the small, tightly wrapped buds along its length, each sealed in overlapping scales against the frost. Inside every bud, he told her, the tree had folded the leaves of next spring months earlier, so that nothing would be left to chance when the warm weather returned. She held the twig very gently, feeling that she was holding a promise that the whole forest had made to itself.

Near the stream stood a tall grey trunk with no branches and no bark, and yet it was crowded with life: a woodpecker drilled at its side, and old holes served as nests. Dead wood is not the end of a tree's story, Tomas said, because beetles, birds, bats and fungi all depend on it for food and shelter. Mina thought that it looked like a very busy apartment block, with a different family living behind every door.

Tomas knelt in the snow, scraped away a little frozen soil with a trowel, and showed Mina a root veiled in fine, pale threads, almost too thin to see. They belong to fungi, he said, and the best-studied of these partnerships are called mycorrhizal, from old Greek words meaning “fungus” and “root”. Mina bent so close that her breath fogged the soil, and she tried to imagine how many such threads lay beneath the whole wood.

It is a very old trade: the tree pays the fungus in sugar made by its leaves, and the fungus pays the tree in water and minerals such as phosphorus. The fungal threads, Tomas said, are far finer than any root, and many of the trees around them are partnered with fungi in this way, and some would struggle to thrive without them. Mina decided that the soil was far less empty than it looked, and that she had been walking over a market all along.

The threads of a single fungus can spread through the soil and touch the roots of many trees at once, joining them into what people call a mycorrhizal network. In careful experiments, scientists have measured carbon, nutrients and chemical signals passing along such links from one tree to another, and the findings have made many people think differently about a forest. Mina imagined a vast, hidden web running beneath her boots, quietly joining every tree she could see.

Suzanne Simard, a forest scientist, and other researchers have found that the oldest and largest trees are often linked to a great many neighbours, which is why some of them call these giants hub trees or mother trees. Some scientists think such a tree may pass carbon and nutrients along the fungal threads to the young seedlings growing in its shade, giving them a better chance. Tomas looked up at the old oak and said that it was a lovely idea, and that it was still being tested.

Before leaving, Tomas asked her to write in her notebook that scientists agree fungi connect tree roots and that some materials pass between trees, but they do not yet agree on how much this matters. Some researchers think the help given to neighbours may be small, or that trees are mainly competing, and good science, he said, means holding an idea gently until it has been tested again and again. Mina underlined the word “debated” twice, because it seemed to her the most honest word on the page.

Spring crept in as the days lengthened and the soil warmed, and the trees, which had been resting for months, began to stir. Sap climbed through the trunks, the buds swelled and split, and a faint green haze spread through the branches until the whole wood seemed to breathe out. Mina ran ahead along the path, desperate to find out whether her acorn had survived.

By the marker stick, Mina found her acorn cracked open, and from the crack a pale root had pushed out into the soil, thin as a thread and already turning downwards. The first thing a seed does, Tomas told her, is to anchor itself and find water, because a tiny shoot can do nothing without the root that feeds it. She laughed out loud in the empty wood, and the sound startled a wren out of the bushes.

Near its tip, the root was covered in microscopic root hairs, each one a single cell reaching into the gaps between grains of soil to drink in water and dissolved minerals. A full-grown tree has countless such tips, Tomas said, and together they act like a vast, patient sponge. Mina leaned in with her magnifying glass, but the hairs were too fine even for that.

Using a stick, Tomas sketched the roots of the oak in the dust, not plunging straight down like a carrot as Mina had expected, but spreading wide and shallow, often farther than the branches reach. Roots grow towards moisture and away from hard, dry ground, he said, and they feel their way along tiny differences in the soil much as a hand feels in the dark. Mina looked at the drawing and then at the great trunk, trying to picture the hidden half of the tree.

Within days a shoot had pushed out of the soil beside the stick, unfolding two or three small leaves the colour of fresh lettuce. It stood in the deep shade of the great oak, where only flecks of sunlight reached the floor, and Tomas said that many seedlings can wait there for years. Growing a little at a time, they wait for a gap in the canopy, Tomas added, and Mina promised her seedling that she would be patient too.

High overhead the great oak unfolded its leaves, soft and bright and crinkled like paper that had been tightly folded, and the light under the canopy turned to a clear, trembling green. Each leaf, Tomas said, is a small factory that must work hard from the moment it opens. Mina tilted her head back until her neck ached, and she watched the light flicker through the new leaves.

Tomas held a leaf up to the sun and explained photosynthesis: using the energy of light, the green chlorophyll inside the leaf builds sugar out of water from the soil and carbon dioxide from the air. The tree uses that sugar to grow, to repair itself and to power everything it does, and the oxygen left over drifts out into the air that animals breathe. Mina realised that a tree is built, to a surprising degree, out of air and light.

Through her magnifying glass, Mina saw that the underside of the leaf was dotted with minute pores called stomata, each one able to open and close like a tiny pair of lips. They let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out, but they also let water vapour escape, which is a cost the tree must always balance, closing them when the air is dry and the soil is short of water. Mina held her breath, half expecting the leaf to answer, and then she laughed at herself for being so quiet.

The water that the roots take in climbs through narrow tubes in the wood called xylem, all the way to the highest leaves, without any heart to pump it. As water evaporates from the leaves, it pulls on the water behind it in an unbroken chain, because water molecules cling to one another, and so the whole column is drawn upward like a drink through a very long straw. Mina put her ear against the trunk, half hoping to hear the water moving upward, but the oak kept its secret.

The sugar made in the leaves has to be shared with the whole tree, and it travels down through a second set of living tubes, the phloem, which lie just beneath the bark. Roots, trunk and fungal partners are all fed by this slow river of sweetness, and that is why cutting a ring through the bark can starve the roots even when the wood inside is untouched. Mina took her hand off the trunk, very respectfully, as if she had interrupted something important.

The branches had filled with life: a pair of blue tits carried moss to a hole in the trunk, bees worked the blossom of a wild cherry, and the oak itself hung out long yellow catkins. The oak does not depend on insects, Tomas said, because it scatters its pollen on the wind, and with luck some grains will reach another oak's flowers and start next year's acorns. Mina sneezed, and he laughed and said that she was now part of the process.

Mina found a leaf so riddled with holes that it looked like lace, and a fat green caterpillar sat on it, still chewing. A tree cannot run away or hide, Tomas said, so it has to defend itself where it stands, and over a very long time trees have developed an astonishing range of defences. In many species these include bitter chemicals in the leaves, which make them less pleasant, and sometimes less safe, to eat.

When a leaf is chewed, some trees give off a cloud of airborne chemicals, and in laboratory and field experiments neighbouring plants that detected them have sometimes responded by raising their own defences. Whether this counts as a warning, in the sense of a message sent on purpose, is something scientists still argue about, for the chemicals may simply be a by-product of the injury. Tomas smiled and said that either way it showed that trees are far more sensitive than they look.

The same airborne chemicals may do a second job, because some studies show that certain wasps and insect-eating birds are drawn to the smell of a damaged leaf, and they hunt the caterpillars responsible. In this way a tree under attack seems to call in its own defenders, though it is more accurate to say that the animals have learned to read the signs. Mina wondered whether a forest was less like a crowd of strangers and more like a village.

By midsummer the fields beyond the trees shimmered with heat, yet under the canopy the air felt cool and damp, as though they had stepped into a different country. The leaves cast a deep shade, and the water they release as vapour takes heat with it when it evaporates, so that a forest acts as a natural air conditioner for the creatures sheltering inside. Tomas sat down on a root and let out a long, contented sigh, and Mina sat beside him and drank from her bottle.

One afternoon a summer storm rolled over the hills, and Mina and Tomas watched from a shelter of rock as the treetops swayed and roared. Trees that are regularly shaken by the wind tend to grow shorter and thicker, with stronger trunks and roots, Tomas said, so that a sheltered tree can be more fragile than one that has weathered many gales. When the rain stopped, the whole wood dripped and glittered, and the air smelled sharply of wet leaves and earth.

Beyond the stream the forest changed, for here an old fire had passed through, leaving blackened trunks and a floor crowded with bright young plants. Fire is a natural part of many forests, Tomas explained, and some trees survive it thanks to thick bark, while a few pines keep their seeds in cones that open only in the heat. But fire is also dangerous, he added, and a great many fires today are started by people.

On the way home they came upon an enormous beech that the storm had brought down, its roots standing upright like a wall of earth torn out of the ground, with stones still caught in the tangle. Where the tree had stood there was now a bright gap in the canopy, and light poured down onto a floor that had lived in shadow for decades. Tomas looked sad for a moment, and then he said that for the young trees waiting below, this was the best day of their lives.

Fungi, beetles and bacteria had already gone to work on the fallen trunk, which would take years, even decades, to rot away entirely, and moss and bright mushrooms were spreading along its length. Decay is not the opposite of life, Tomas said, but the way a forest recycles its wealth, returning the nutrients locked in the wood gradually to the soil. Seedlings often sprout along a rotting log as if along a nursery shelf, he added, and Mina wrote the words nurse log in her notebook and drew a small tree growing from one.

One evening, in the lamplight, Tomas opened a book at a page showing a bristlecone pine, its trunk twisted and silvered by wind and its roots clinging to a bare, dry mountainside in the western United States. Some of these trees have lived for more than four thousand years, and the oldest known are nearly five thousand years old. They grow slowly in poor soil, he said, and that slowness, together with their hard, resin-rich wood, may be part of their secret.

The next page showed the coast redwoods of California, and the tallest known among them rise more than one hundred metres from the forest floor, higher than a skyscraper of about thirty storeys. These giants live along a strip where cool fog rolls in from the Pacific, and research has shown that they can drink some of that fog through their leaves. Tomas added that this is a useful trick for a tree whose highest branches are so far from its roots, and Mina tried to imagine standing at the foot of one.

Autumn came round again, and the oak let its leaves fall exactly as it had a year before, though now Mina could name almost everything that was happening inside it. She no longer saw a crowd of separate trees, but a slow, tangled community of roots, fungi, insects, birds and rot, all dependent on one another. Tomas walked a little behind her and let her lead, as he had begun to do some weeks before without saying so.

The stick had faded to grey, but the seedling beside it was green and upright, a year older and perhaps a hand's breadth taller, with a bud already formed for the spring. It had survived frost, hungry animals and deep shade, and Tomas reminded her that most acorns never get this far, so that the oak above them had needed only one or two of its many acorns to succeed. Mina measured it against her palm, and although it was hardly bigger than her hand, she felt unreasonably proud.

Photosynthesis has a consequence far beyond the forest: as trees grow, they draw carbon dioxide out of the air and lock the carbon into their trunks, branches, roots and the soil around them. Forests therefore act as great stores of carbon, and when they are burned, cleared or left to dry out, some of it returns to the air as the same gas that is warming the planet. Tomas said quietly that keeping old forests standing is among the most useful things people can do, although it cannot replace cutting pollution.

Mina had come to see that a forest is far more than a crowd of trees, for it shelters countless animals, holds the soil in place with its roots and helps to keep streams clear and clean. Rain that falls on a wooded slope is slowed by the leaves and soaked up by the soil, Tomas said, rather than rushing away all at once. She watched a deer lower its head to drink and tried not to move.

Tomas told her that planting trees is a fine thing to do, provided that the right kinds are planted in the right places and are looked after for years afterwards. Protecting the forests that already exist matters just as much, because an old forest holds soil, fungal threads and ancient trees that no planting can replace in a lifetime. He said that every wood, however small, is worth a defender, and that she could begin with the one at the end of her own street.

Before they turned for home, Tomas gave her two rules that a forester learns early: leave deadwood where it lies, and walk lightly. Deadwood feeds countless creatures and fungi, he explained, and soil that is crushed by many boots becomes hard for roots to grow in, so both rules were really about respect. They were small rules, he admitted, and Mina said them aloud twice, as though learning a spell.

Mina chose a sound acorn from the path, pressed it into the soft earth at the edge of the wood, and pushed a new stick in beside it, just as she had done a year before. She would be old before it stood as high as the great oak, and perhaps this seed would never make it at all, yet she felt as if she had joined something far larger than herself. Tomas put a hand on her shoulder, and above them the forest went quietly on growing.
